parole.significato: Independent research, observation of something (as opposed to second hand accounts)
parole.testo: From New Latin autopsia, from Ancient Greek αὐτοψῐ́ᾱ (autopsĭ́ā, “seeing with one's own eyes”).

parole.significato: Arachis (genus within the family Fabaceae – flowering plants, of which the peanut is the best known)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from New Latin arachis, from Ancient Greek (see ἄρακος (árakos), ἀράχιδνα (arákhidna)). Compare Russian ара́хис (aráxis).
From New Latin hygiena, from Ancient Greek ὑγιεινή (hugieinḗ). Compare Russian гигие́на (gigijéna), Belarusian гігіе́на (hihijéna), Polish higiena.

From New Latin ēlectrica, from Latin ēlectrum (“amber”), from Ancient Greek ἤλεκτρον (ḗlektron, “amber”). The Latin term was apparently used first with the sense “electrical” in 1600 by the English physician and scientist, William Gilbert in his work De Magnete.
Derived via Western European languages from New Latin neurosis, from Ancient Greek νεῦρον (neûron) + -ωσις (-ōsis).

From New Latin neurologia, from Ancient Greek νεῦρον (neûron, “sinew, tendon, cord”) + -логія (-lohija) from Ancient Greek -λογία (-logía, “study of”). Compare Russian невроло́гия (nevrológija), Belarusian неўрало́гія (njewralóhija), Polish neurologia.

Borrowed from New Latin nostalgia, coined from Ancient Greek νόστος (nóstos, “returning home”) + ἄλγος (álgos, “pain”). Compare Russian ностальги́я (nostalʹgíja), Belarusian настальгі́я (nastalʹhíja).

From New Latin ontologia (1606, Ogdoas Scholastica, by Jacob Lorhard (Lorhardus)), from Ancient Greek ὤν (ṓn, “on”), present participle of εἰμί (eimí, “being, existing, essence”) + -λογία (-logía). With -ло́гія (-lóhija) ending. Compare Russian онтоло́гия (ontológija), Belarusian антало́гія (antalóh

Derived via Western European languages from New Latin ornithologia, from Ancient Greek ὄρνῑθος (órnīthos) + -λογία (-logía). With -ло́гія (-lóhija) ending. Compare Russian орнитоло́гия (ornitológija), Belarusian арніталогія (arnitalóhija), Polish ornitologia.
Borrowed from New Latin peritonitis, ultimately from Ancient Greek περιτόναιον (peritónaion) and -ῖτις (-îtis). Compare Russian перитони́т (peritonít), Belarusian перытані́т (pjerytanít).
Borrowed from New Latin pneumonia, from Ancient Greek πνευμονία (pneumonía). Compare Russian пневмони́я (pnevmoníja), Belarusian пнеўмані́я (pnjewmaníja).
From New Latin psychosis, from Ancient Greek ψυχή (psukhḗ, “vital spirit, soul”) + -ωσις (-ōsis, “state, abnormal condition, or action”).
From New Latin spora, from Ancient Greek σπορά (sporá, “sowing, seed”).
From New Latin tachycardia, from Ancient Greek ταχύς (takhús, “swift”) + καρδία (kardía, “heart”).
From New Latin therapīa, from Ancient Greek θεραπεία (therapeía, “service, medical treatment”), from θεραπεύω (therapeúō, “I serve, treat medically”).

Borrowed from New Latin Utopia, the name of a fictional island, possessing a seemingly perfect socio-politico-legal system in the book Utopia (1516) by Sir Thomas More. Coined from Ancient Greek οὐ (ou, “not, no”) + τόπος (tópos, “place, region”).
Derived via Western European languages from New Latin phasis, from Ancient Greek φάσις (phásis).
Borrowed from New Latin phōsphorus, from Ancient Greek φωσφόρος (phōsphóros, “light-bearing”), from φῶς (phôs, “light”) + φέρω (phérō, “to bear, carry”).

From New Latin chronologia, from Ancient Greek χρόνος (khrónos, “chronos”) + -λογία (-logía). With -ло́гія (-lóhija) ending. Compare Russian хроноло́гия (xronológija), Belarusian хранало́гія (xranalóhija), Polish chronologia.
Borrowed from New Latin hypochondria, from Ancient Greek ῠ̔ποχόνδρῐος (hŭpokhóndrĭos). Compare Russian ипохо́ндрия (ipoxóndrija), Belarusian іпахо́ндрыя (ipaxóndryja), Polish hipochondria.
